Shreyas Srinivas said:

As far a lean goes, mathlib is the defacto standard. In fact going outside the formalization world into pure math, lean is the biggest name among ITPs. CSLib doesn’t haven’t that status and will probably never get there.

I'm not disagreeing per se with any of this, but we are discussing a very limited scope of libraries in the Mathlib ecosystem. To my knowledge, nobody has ever claimed claim that CSLib is "the" computer science library of all ITPs.

CSLib makes its claim right in its repository description

image_C2BABE3D-AFD3-4574-A751-558B4806635D_1774265656.jpeg

Also further down in README

image_9E0B2BD6-CBA8-48E4-9C71-C5415EC47641_1774265738.jpeg

That’s a claim to exclusivity which doesn’t hold even inside the intersection of lean and CS community.
Anyway I’d like to return to the importance of creating explicity standards rather than proxy standards via merging into specific libraries. This seems to be of importance across subjects

This is drifting off-topic, but I do not think that is a reasonable interpretation and feel obliged to respond. This is stylized after Mathlib's description: "The math library of Lean 4". Would you interpret that as meaning it assumes to be the only math library of all ITPs? Just like Mathlib, we are aiming to providing a centralized library of computer science. It is expected and welcome for others to use it downstream in their own developments, or not at all if they so choose.
Can we move this to a different topic please?
I’d like to respond but not take up space in this topic.
I don't have permission, but would be happy for an admin to move this to the CSLib channel.
7 messages were moved here from #general > The role of AI companies in large formalisation projects by Riccardo Brasca.
7 messages were moved from this topic to #CSLib > CSLib Readme by Riccardo Brasca.

I have several objections to the claim that CSLib is "the" computer science library for lean.

  1. Firstly CSLib does not serve the same role in CS as mathlib does for math. Most CS projects neither ought to, nor seem to want to upstream anything to CSLib.
  2. CS is a much broader and more splintered field. It is worth asking if a monolithic library even makes sense.
  3. Unlike mathlib, CS has a long history of formalizations and we will probably never agree on "the one correct way" to formalize many things. Heck, we have arguments about something as basic as algorithms. This is an active topic of research and we have actively used ITPs for two decades to actually express this research as opposed to just post-hoc formalization.
  4. The most pressing concern is that of legitimacy. By claiming a similar role as mathlib, CSLib is laying claim to mathlib's legitimacy as the ultimate destination of all CS formalizations. We have seen this in the other thread where people assumed that the standard for great formalizations will be getting upstreamed into these libraries. I don't think such a claim is appropriate for CSLib yet, nor will it ever be. In our field, formalization is a way of building new research ideas and has been so for a very long time in some areas like PL.
A more tone-neutral phrasing would be "A computer science library in Lean"

Even if you ignore the first three claims, the legitimacy claim matters, especially since this discussion just diverged from one where we were talking about legitimate formalizations being ones accepted by these libraries.. If the lean community is going to put out a statement on formalization standards that gives CSLib some claim to superior legitimacy from a quality perspective on par with mathlib, this is not going to be well-received on the CS side. At least it will be ignored to a point. For example, I am already aware that some researchers/communities want their own libraries, and integration with CSLib is not a priority for them. I can completely understand this is not a popular opinion in this community. I also dislike fragmentation. But claims to being "the" something require very strong justification, broad consensus, and backing, which simply doesn't exist in CS as a whole.
Maybe a more emphatic phrasing is "A consolidated CS library for lean" or "A unified library of undergraduate computer science"

Even if the long term vision is to achieve a mathlib-like status, that will come from years of consolidating formalizations into CSLib. Maybe at that point, CSLib would be justified with using the definite article. But that justification does not exist yet.
I don't see the point of this bikeshedding, and for CSLib to downplay itself. Fake it until you make it.
This is not bikeshedding. It is consequential to people who publish their formalisations in lean if the community says "good formalisations" correlate to being upstreamed to CSLib.

As always I don't presume to speak for all the maintainers, but my thoughts. I think the most legitimate point you have is

It is worth asking if a monolithic library even makes sense.

I certainly don't claim to have a definitive answer to this! I do think there are some qualitative differences in formalizing CS that are interesting to consider, though I think you are drawing some artificial divisions. To be more concrete though, we simply have seen the success that Mathlib has had with its monorepo design, and we want to try and see what that looks like with CSLib. Just like with any open source formalization effort, anyone is free to diverge, to use part or none of what we offer.

We fully understand that this is a brand new effort (less than a year old) and I am certainly not in support of marking inclusion in CSLib as a singular mark of legitimacy for a Lean formalization, as I personally don't think this even makes sense for Mathlib. To my memory, over the Lean 3 years Mathlib's description varied from "standard library" to "mathematical components". Maybe something like "computer science components" would be analogous, but to be honest I feel as if what you've written above is unfairly attributing a lot of intent to the presence of a definite article. Nowhere have we requested to "[lay] claim to mathlib's legitimacy as the ultimate destination of all CS formalizations".
I am aware that you haven't made the request. I don't attribute any motives to CSLib.

I am merely pointing out that the (non-ITP-building) lean audience, largely coming from the math side these days, appears to perceive things in a certain way, as evidenced by Joseph's suggestion the other thread. I am also pointing out that we can avoid this perception by adopting a slightly neutral phrasing.
We are communicating to several audiences simultaneously and in this context strong claims are interpreted very differently by people from different backgrounds.
Also for those who might not see the other thread, the context is here : #general > The role of AI companies in large formalisation projects @ 💬
